HMTD (hexamethylenetriperoxidediamine)

This repository documents the historical discovery and synthesis procedures of HMTD , with the original sources provided as PDFs. Some of the articles were originally written in German. English translations are also included.

I wrote this repository on my own instead of using AI. Claude Opus refused my prompt asking for HMTD due to safety concerns. No matter how I tried to jailbreak Opus, I couldn’t bypass its safeguards. It sucked… :(

Brief History

HMTD is known for a high explosive organic peroxide compound. It was originally intended for use in detonators, but owing to its instability, it failed to displace mercury fulminate, which was the prevailing choice at the time. Today, its facile and inexpensive synthesis has made it a component of choice in HMEs and terrorist activities.

HMTD was first synthesized in 1855 by the German chemist L. Legler. His article concerned the oxidation of diethyl ether, but he serendipitously obtained “Lamp acid” by oxidizing diethyl ether with O₂ over Pt under harsh conditions. He subsequently treated Lamp acid with ammonia to afford HMTD. Notably, Legler was unable to correctly identify the structure of Lamp acid, and his synthetic method was inefficient; he reported obtaining only a trace amount of HTMD.

In 1897, J. U. Nef identified the Lamp acid obtained by Legler as a trimer of BHMP. He also elucidated the mechanism of Legler’s oxidation: diethyl ether is oxidized to give formaldehyde, hydrogen peroxide, acetaldehyde, acetic acid, and formic acid, among which hydrogen peroxide and formaldehyde react to form BHMP (Lamp acid).

In 1900, A. Baeyer and V. Villiger, building on Nef’s work, provided an accurate account of how Legler had obtained HMTD through the oxidation of diethyl ether. They also determined the chemical structure of HMTD, which remains the accepted structure today. Furthermore, they modified the synthetic procedure by employing ammonium sulfate, formaldehyde, and hydrogen peroxide. However, they did not report the yield of HT obtained by this method.

In 1912, C. von Girsewald reported an efficient synthesis of HMTD based on the decomposition of hexamine with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of citric acid. This method is still widely used today and remains the most efficient route known. He reported a yield of 64%. Through explosion experiments, he also demonstrated that HMTD is more hazardous than mercury fulminate.

Synthetic method

Here, I provide two detailed synthesis procedures. The original method of C. von Girsewald, and a slightly modified modern adaptation.

From C. von Girsewald

If 28 g hexamethylenetetramine and 42 g citric acid are dissolved in 140 g of 30% hydrogen peroxide, the solution warms somewhat and gradually deposits abundant amounts of hexamethylene triperoxide diamine as small, regular, rhombic crystals. Washed with water and then with alcohol, one obtains 27.5 g, corresponding to a yield of 66% of theory, referred to hexamethylenetetramine.

From J. Phys. Chem. A, Vol. 105, No. 38, 2001

A 125 mL three-neck flask equipped with a paddle-type microstirrer was charged with 7.00 g (50 mmol) of hexamethylenetetramine and 23 mL of 50% H2O2 and chilled to ∼0 °C (ice/NaCl). While being stirred,11.5 g (54.7 mmol) citric acid monohydrate was added in 10 small portions over the course of 2 h. The clear solution was stirred at ∼0 °C for an additional 8 h; the ice-bath was removed,and the solution was allowed to warm slowly to room temperature. The resultant opaque mixture was stirred for an additional 2 h, the micro-stirrer was removed, and the flask containing the product was re-chilled in ice for 30 min. The white crystalline material was gravity filtered and then rinsed with 3 × 50 mL ice water, followed by 2 × 20 mL ice-cold CH3OH rinses. The crystalline material and filter paper was dried in a vacuum desiccator (CaSO4) overnight to afford 5.75 g (27.6 mmol; 55%) product: mp ) 152-153 °C (exp.) (lit. mp ) 144-145 °C;17 154 °C18); 1H NMR (CDCl3): δ 4.80; 13C NMR δ 90.44.

Reaction mechanism

The HTMD reaction mechanism proceeds in two steps; the decomposition of hexamine, and the reaction of the decomposition products with hydrogen peroxide.

Fisrt step: In aqueous condition, Hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) undergoes hydrolysis to formaldehyde and ammonia. (although the reaction mechanism is depicted as equilibrium. The use of citric acid in this system shifts the equilibrium to the right.) The reaction proceeds through repeated iminium ion mediated C-N cleavage. 1. N-protionation occurrs. Hexamine is a weak monoacidic base. Rapidly, reversivle protonation at one bridehead nitrogen gives HMTAH+. 2. Ring opening to an iminium ion. Assisted by the lone pair of an adjacent N, the C-N+ bond heterolyses.This opens the cage and generates a R2N+=CH2 together with a pendant secondary amine. 3. Nucleophilic addtion of water to the imminium carbon then gives a hemiaminal, R2N-CH2-OH. 4. N-protonation of the hemiaminal, fllowed by the C-N cleavage driven by the hydroxyl oxygen, expels the amine and releases formaldehyde.

These steps repeat for each methylene unit. They pass through progressively degraded intermediates: 1,3,5,7-tetraazabicyclo[3.3.1]nonane (TBN), triazinane-type and aclyclic aminomethyl species, methanediamin, and aminomethanol. Each nitrogen is finally released as ammonia.

After the decomposition of HMTA, protonation activates the formaldehyde generated by this decomposition toward nucleophilic attack by ammonia tp give the corresponding imine. This step is also an equilibrium process.

Second step: First, formaldehyde is activated by the acid from citric acid and undergoes nucleophilic attack by hydrogen peroxide to afford bis(hydroxymethyl)peroxide (BHMP). Subsequently, the imine is similarly activated by the acid and reacts with hydrogen peroxide to provide bis(aminomethyl) peroxide (BAMP).Finally, condensation of two equivalents pf BHMP with one equivalent of BAMP, followed by cyclization, yields HMTD.

Mitigation

HMTD is unstable, and its decomposition can occasionally trigger an explosive reation. Understanding appropriate mitigation measures is therefore essential for safe handling. HMTD decomposed readily in the presence of diluted acids such as 36% HCl or 65% H2SO4, whereas concentrated acids like 98% H2SO4 induce detonation. Only dilute acids must be used.
